A Racket in the Racket Club.
TWO OF THE MEMBERS FINED FOR CAPTURING
A POLICEMAN.
A POLICEMAN.
[New York Times, yesterday.]
Carlson of No. 212 west

John Carlson, of No. 212 west One-Hundred-and-Twenty-fifth street, entered Rushton's drugstore, in Sixth avenue, on Thursday evening, to make some purchases. On turning to pay for the articles he had bought he discovered that his purse, containing $3, which he alleged he had laid down on the counter of the store, was missing. Upon making known his loss the proprietor of the store informed him that a colored servant in the employ of the Racket Club had left the place with a purse in his hand.

Mr. Carlson is a nervous individual, and upon receiving this information he at once jumped to the conclusion that the purse carried off was his property. Hastening to the Twenty-ninth-Precinct station-house, he reported the loss of his purse and detailed his suspicions as to its theft, and Policeman Ringler was sent to arrest the suspected colored servant of the Club, whose name is John Whitehurst.

At the time of the officer's arrival Whitehurst was serving some of the members of the Club. He expressed surprise at the arrest, but declared his willingness to accompany the officer, at the same time requesting an opportunity to change his clothes. The officer declined to let his prisoner out of his sight, and followed him into an ante-room. In the mean time several of the younger members of the Club were laughing and joking over their servant's arrest, and carried away by a spirit of mischief, some of them locked the door of the room in which were the officer and his prisoner.

As soon as Policeman Ringler heard the key turn in the lock he became greatly excited, and, throwing up a window, he shouted to Carlson, who was waiting below, to go to the station-house and report the condition of affairs. On being informed of the state of the case, Captain Williams dispatched Roundsman Cowley and eighteen policemen to the club-house, and on arriving there the officers took James Aymar, Thomas Bach, and William S. Alley into custody. The released Ringler and his prisoner, Whitehurst, also found their way to the station-house.

Soon after the arrest a number of carriages drove up before the station-house, and there were a number of applications to see the prisoners. Captain Williams, however, refused to allow them to be seen. Strenuous efforts were made by friends to find a police justice, but in vain.

When the prisoners were arraigned yesterday morning before Justice Ford, in the Jefferson Market Police Court, they were ably represented by counsel—Elihu Root, Gilbert M. Speir, Jr., and Charles S. Spencer appearing for the defence. There not being the slightest evidence against the colored prisoner, he was discharged. James Aymar and Thomas Bach were fined $10 each for interfering with Policeman Ringler while in the discharge of his duty. No evidence was forthcoming against William S. Alley, and the case against him was accordingly dismissed.

The Police at the Racquet Club.
The conduct of the police at the Racquet Club on Thursday evening has had one good result at least. It has aroused an interest in the law relating to personal liberty. Club men want to know all about the right to make arrests with warrant and without warrant. The unfortunate experience of the two young gentlemen who were taken into custody may thus prove serviceable to others in suggesting what to do and what not to do under similar circumstances.

These two members of the club, with a friend, were quietly dining together, when a policeman entered their room and undertook to arrest the negro servant who was waiting on them. The officer said the man was charged with having stolen a pocketbook from the drug store on the ground floor of the club building. He did not pretend that the crime had been committed in his presence, and he had no warrant for the apprehension of the accused person. Nevertheless he proposed to take him to the station house at once. The gentlemen in the room remonstrated with the officer. They denied his legal authority to make an arrest for such an offence without a warrant. He says they then locked him in, and although they dispute the truth of that statement, it seems certain that they gave him to understand he could not leave the apartment with his prisoner.

All this time the complainant, whose lost, strayed, or stolen pocketbook was responsible for the whole trouble, stood waiting outside the club on the sidewalk. The baffled policeman leaned out of the window and informed him of the predicament he was in. The complainant carried the news to Capt. ALEXANDER S. WILLIAMS of the Twenty-ninth Precinct, and in a few moments the Bacquet Club was invaded by a roundsman and four patrolmen, who came to the relief of their comrade. This force speedily escorted the accused servant and two of the gentlemen who had interfered in his behalf to the police station, where they remained until next morning. The servant was discharged by the magistrate, who was satisfied that a mistake had been made in his case, and the two members of the club were fined $10 each for resisting the officer.

The law relative to arrests without a warrant is stated as follows in the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The first subdivision does not apply to the case under consideration, because the policeman was not present when the alleged crime was committed.

The second subdivision does not apply, because, even if the charge against the servant was true, it amounted only to petit larceny, which is a misdemeanor, and not a felony.

The third subdivision does not apply, because it also relates only to felonies.

If a felony had been committed, and the officer had good reasons for suspecting the servant of the Racquet Club to be the guilty party, his authority to arrest him without a warrant would have been indisputable. But a felony had not been committed. The complaint which was preferred against the servant was for a misdemeanor only, and the Police Justice did not hold him even on that charge. Under the circumstances, and in view of the final disposition of the case by the magistrate, the attempt to arrest the accused waiter without a warrant appears clearly to have been unlawful.

If it was unlawful, it was wholly outside and in violation of the officer's duty, and we are unable to perceive how the Police Justice could have come to the conclusion that the gentlemen who interposed and sought to prevent the officer from doing an illegal act were punishable. The case would be different if they had obstructed an officer in discharging, or attempting to discharge, a duty of his office. An act that the law forbids cannot be viewed as a duty. The servant would have been justified in using such force as might be necessary to prevent the attempted arrest, and we recall no rule of law which makes it illegal for others to aid him in resisting apprehension which he may lawfully resist himself.

THE RACQUET CLUB ARRESTS.

When the officer told me that he wanted me for stealing a pocket-book from Rusiton's drug store, I said that I would go with him if he would wait till I saw my employers, Mr. Aymar and Mr. Bach; and he walked into the dining-room with me. Thomas C. Bach testified that he was a lawyer, and not a member of the Racquet Club. He said:

I said that I would send for Captain Williams, and if he said the arrest was proper that it would be satisfactory to us. He answered me in a way that I cannot repeat, as I do not speak in that manner. I replied, "No man talks to me this way in my own room," and he asked me if I intended to murder him. I told him that I did not. He asked me if I would let him out. I said yes. He then asked me if he could take his prisoner, and I said "Yes, if Captain Williams says so." When the other officers came I did not know they were officers, and I did not open the door. As we were about opening the door they pushed it in. A TILT BETWEEN WEAVER AND HUBBARD—THE LIFE OF POLITICS.

Mineola, June 20.—The first gun of the campaign was fired to-day. Gen. J. B. Weaver, of Iowa, and Gov. Hubbard, of Tyler, addressed our citizens in a joint discussion this evening. The topics discussed were, first, the financial system of the government; second, the railway corporations; third, the bonded debt—shall it be paid off or perpetuated? Gen. Weaver opened a formal statement of these questions, with the views of the green-back party thereon, and a challenge to Gov. Hubbard to define the position of the democracy on these issues, and to answer sundry accusations against the democratic party. Hubbard replied in a speech of one hour and a half in duration. Gen. Weaver closed the argument. Both speakers were heartily cheered, and both parties claimed the victoryr One thousand people or more composed the audience. Among the notables present were Col. Kilgore, of Wills Point, and Hon. Horace Chilton, of Tyler, both candidates for congress in this district. Messrs. Chilton and Kilgore both purposed to answer Gen. Weaver but were prevented by the approach of night.

BLOODY TERMINATION OF EMANCIPATION DAY.

Houston, June 20.—A fatal row occurred just before daylight this morning at the emancipation celebration grounds. They killed a white man named Chas. Witham. Four shots passed simultaneously through his body and head. They also wounded deputy marshal Wm. Glass, shooting the latter as he stopped to pick up the latter. The ball entered in the rear of the left shoulder and was extracted from the side of the neck. He will likely recover. The shots fired at Witham came as if in a volley. He died instantly. A negro named Harry Nelson was killed, it is supposed by a stray shot. A negro named Frank H. Spencer, and a negro woman were accidentally wounded by shots from the negroes. Several white men were ejected from the grounds by the negroes. Much indignation is felt by Witham's friends. He was a member of the Typographical Union, and treasurer of Houston lodge of young native Houstonians. Apprehension among the negroes to-night, broke up a continuation of the celebration.

Washington June 20.—Under the bill which passed the house authorizing the secretary of the treasury to report to congress the claims of states and territories for expenditures made in repelling invasions and suppressing Indian hostilities, and which now goes to the president for approval, the state of Texas will claim about $150,000, Kansas about $240,000, Nevada about $323,000, California about $400,000, Colorado about $70,000 and Oregon about $50,000.

New York, June 20.—The freight handlers' strike is spreading. This morning a large body of them passed down West street to the battery. Later in the day the laboers in the Erie and New York and New Haven freight houses quit work, and the warehouses were closed. Albion, June 20.—The Johnson harvester works, of Brockport, were totally burned last night. The loss is estimated at $300,000; insured for $200,000 in several companies. London, June 20.—The lord Mayor of London appeared in the house of commons this afternoon in his official robes, and presented a petition of the corporation of Dublin against the repression bill. He attempted to address the house on the question, when he was called to order.

London, June 20.—A very large amount of British import trade, from Egypt, is in cotton. The stopping of the business there will be keenly felt in Lancashire, especially at Bolton, where many mills use Egyptian cotton exclusively.

Shooting in Texas.
HOUSTON, June 21.—Early yesterday morning on the Emancipation grounds, Chas. F. Witham was fired upon by negroes and instantly killed. As Deputy Marshal Glass was lifting the body of the dead man he was fired upon, a bullet entering his right shoulder and coming out of the side of his neck. A colored boy was killed by a stray bullet and a negro named Spencer was shot in the back of the neck. John Glass, brother of the deputy, went to his assistance, but was disarmed and ejected from the grounds. Annotorious negro politician, Ed. Jamison, has been arrested as one of the murderers of Witham, and Frank Bufford as being party to the shooting of Deputy Glass.
emancipation-day-houston-1882-06.A16: Last Monday the colored people of Houston wound up their celebration of emancipation day in a manner not at all surprising to any one who is familiar with the character and natural instincts of the majority of this race. After listening to a speech from E. J. Davis, ex-radical governor of Texas, in which he told them that he could plainly note their wonderful progress in the past seventeen years from the intelligent faces and fine personal appearance of the men and women before him, they wound up their day's festivities by committing a cold-blooded murder. Their victim was Mr. C. F. Witham, an attachee of the Daily Post, well and favorably known in Houston where he had been born and raised. His body was riddled with bullets, and for no other reason in the world but because he chose to visit the grounds in company with several others, among them Deputy Sheriff Glass, who was shot through the shoulder while in the act of raising his dead companion. Several others were shot, not dangerously, and a negro boy, while running to escape the flying bullets, was killed by a stray ball. Two negroes, supposed to be the leaders of the affair, have been arrested, and it is to be hoped that a speedy retribution may be meted out to them.

JOHNSON's harvester works, Brockport, N. Y., employing 450 men, burned on the 20th. Loss, $500,000; insurance, $200,-000. One man perished.

[SPECIAL TO THE SENTINEL.]

Chicago, June 14.—Specials from Washington say the attention of Republican members of Congress has been called to the significant proceeding on the part of Democratic Congressional Committee in getting ready for the coming campaign. A pamphlet has been prepared in the guise of a public document, being indorsed, "Part of the Congressional Record," and is permitted to go free through the mails. The pamphlet contains articles of speeches made for and against Chinese immigration, so selected as best to suit the Democratic purpose. The evident intention is to place the Republican party in the light of an enemy to the welfare and interest of free American labor. The first part of the pamphlet is devoted to extracts from the speeches of the Democratic party. The first part of the pamphlet is devoted to extracts from the speeches of Rosecrans, Cassidy, Brady, Flower, Tucker, Deuster, Buckner, Richardson, Blount, Curtin, Townshead and McLane, all Democrats. The Chinese Restriction Law is claimed to be a Democratic measure, originated and passed by Democratic votes, with the help of an insignificant number of Republicans. The Morey letter is again displayed, carefully concealing the exposure made by that forgery. The extracts from Democratic speeches are those which are best calculated to make the poor laborer believe the Democratic party is his friend and protector, and the Republican party his enemy. Quotations from Republican speeches are made so as to convey wrong impressions; they are torn from the connection with other issues fair between the two parties. The Democratic Committee are having the pamphlet printed in large numbers for use among the laboring classes.

Labor Troubles.

St. Louis, June 14.—President Garrett of the Amalgamated Association held a secret conference with the strikers this evening. It is understood that they refused to listen to his advice and will continue the strike.

Cohoes, June 14.—To-day the Harmony mills again closed. Not one additional operative joined the ten who returned to work on Monday under the 10 per cent reduction. A meeting of the company will be held to-morrow.

Cleveland, June 14.—The Police Commissioners appointed twenty-five special policemen, and are bound to maintain order about the striking precinct. They have also decided to guard the militia.
Eastern Miscellany.
Kokoma (Ind.), June 14.—The Green-backers of this (Eleventh) District nominated Evan Thompson, a farmer, for Congress.

Salem (Dakota), June 14.—Six cases of smallpox have developed at Bridgewater, on the line of the Milwaukee and St. Paul extension. Salem has quarantined against Bridgewater. No trains stop at the infected town and no mail is taken thence.

St. Paul, June 14.—There are half a dozen cases of smallpox in Minneapolis, and there is quite a scare there. The Webster school has been closed. Few fatalities have occurred.

CHESTERFIELD (N. H.), June 14.—The body of Geo. R. Conley, the operatic singer, was found in Spofford Lake this morning. The remains will be sent to New York.

Guiteau Wants Commutation.
WASHINGTON, June 14.—Guiteau, at his last interview with Reed, exacted a promise that Reed would call on the President and urge a commutation of sentence. He instructed Reed to shake his fist in the President's face and demand protection for him as God's man, who saved the country and made Arthur President. Reed's last appeal for Guiteau has been placed in the hands of Justice Bradley of the United States Supreme Court. It is practically the same as that made before Justice Gray and refused by him. There is no probability that the writ of habeas corpus will be granted.

More Indian Troubles.

Omaha, June 14.—A company of cavalry left Fort Sidney, Nebraska, last evening for McKinney, Wyoming, to reinforce the garrison. General Crook learns from the commandant there that it was rumored 1,500 Indians were on Powder River, below old Fort Kinney, but some miles from the present fort, and that 100 lodges of Indians were on Rock Creek. Stock men report that these Indians are killing cattle and threatening to attack the herders. The commandant has not heard from his messenger, sent to obtain actual facts. General Crook deemed it advisable to send troops.

Severe Rain Storm in Indiana.

INDIANAPOLIS June 14.—The severest storm of the season occurred last night. Two inches of rain fell. The city east of the Union Depot is flooded. Along the railway tracks northwest, up Pennsylvania, Delaware and Alabama streets, the cellars are rapidly filling. Fifteen or twenty persons were standing on the platform over Pogueo Run, when it gave way and threw them into the water. Some were rescued; others passed through the culvert safely, while still others are supposed to be drowned. It is impossible to give the number lost.

A Mob Metes Out Justice to Oscar M. Garrett.
GREENSBURG, IND., April 25.—The last chapter in the exciting life of Oscar M. Garrett is now closed, and the murderer of two men and the instrument of untold family misery and shame has at last paid the penalty of his crimes. Oscar M. Garrett was one month ago tried as an accessory to the murder of John M. Walton, a wealthy farmer, living near St. Paul, and contrary to the expectations of every one was acquitted by a jury of Jennings County farmers. At that time there was much comment on such a verdict, and many threats were made of lynching, but as time passed the affair was forgotten. On his return from Jennings county he was arrested on a charge of arson, and confined in the Decatur county jail, and has been an inmate since that time. The climax was reached this morning, and outraged justice demanded its victim. At 1:30 A.M. the jailer was aroused from his bed by a ring at the door, and at his response was seized by masked men, and ordered to deliver the key to Garrett's cell. His head and body were marked, and his cell covered with blood. HANGING OF GABRETT.
The startling news was flashed over the wires yesterday that Oscar M. Garrett had been taken from the Jail at Greensburg, Decatur County, and hung by a mob. The outrage was committed at about 3 o'clock Monday morning. Last January John M. Walton, a wealthy farmer of Decatur County, was murdered. Circumstances led to the arrest of a negro named Frazier as the guilty person, who confessed the crime, and, in his confession, implicated the wife of the murdered man and Garrett, the man who finally fell a victim to mob violence. In this connection it is well to state that Garrett passed the ordeal of a trial, and was declared by a Juary of his peers "Not guilty." Notwithstanding this, many of his neighbors believed him to have planned the murder, and, quite independent of Frazier's confession, there were many circumstances well calculated to arouse the indignation of his neighbors against him. The foregoing is the case with which the people of Decatur County have had to deal—and the way they have seen proper to dispose of it must of necessity be a disgrace of almost ceaseless duration to Decatur County and to the State of Indiana. For such a crime as the mob committed at Greensburg on Monday morning, the 24th inst., there is no apology. It is beyond the furthermost limits of mitigation. It is a public horror. It is treason to everything of good report in society. It is murderous anarchy, and unless rebuked at all hazards and without reference to cost of time, money and labor, must cover Indiana with shame and confusion. Admitting that circumstances all pointed to Garrett as the instigator of Walton's death; admitting that general rumor, relating to improper relations between Garrett and Mrs. Walton, was well-founded, still the verdict of the Jury pronounced him innocent of the murder of Walton. He was set at liberty, and his rights were as sacred as those of any other citizen of the State. This view of the case makes every man engaged in hanging Garrett a murderer, who should be arrested, convicted and hung. No more serious business now confronts the people of Decatur County than to ferret out the men engaged in hanging Garrett, and if Decatur County is not equal to the task, State authority and State resources should be brought to bear upon the matter, and the good name of the State, by prompt action, should be rescued from the obloquy which the Greensburg mob has brought upon it.

[From Indianapolis Sentinel, April 25.]

GREENSBURG, April 24.---This usually quiet city was startled from a Sabbath night's repose at 2 a.m. with the cry re-echoed through the street, "Garrett's hung by a mob!" Your reporter hastened to the spot in time to see the Sheriff, John W. Stout, cut the rope that held the limp and lifeless form of the once dreaded Oscar Marion Garrett, suspended from a limb of a maple tree standing in the street, immediately in front of the County Jail.

The Jailer, William Toothman, says that at about 2 o'clock an alarm was given at the front door, and upon its being answered three men rushed in and seized him, demanding the keys to Garrett's cell. The Jailer, protesting against such mob violence and refusing the demand, was borne up stairs by the crowd, which followed. Here in the hall, in front of the cell in which Mrs. Walton is confined, the party halted, and, being again refused the keys, a rope was placed around the Jailer's neck and violence threatened him if he should persist in refusing to deliver up Garrett. His wife interceded and begged, "If you must do this terrible deed, break down the doors, and do not implicate us." While this parley was being held a noise was heard in the cell to the left of the hall (better known here as the female department), in which the doomed man has been confined since his rearrest. One of the crowd exclaimed, "The d——d s——n of a b——h is in here," and at once a stalwart proceeded with two blows of a sledge hammer to demolish the clasp and lock—such as ornament country barn doors. The work was soon done, but Garrett was forewarned. He knew his time had come. The first man entering was met with a blow from a chair, which felled him to the floor. But immediately three of the mob rushed in, and overpowering the prisoner, he was dragged by the feet down a flight of stone steps. At the landing he was placed upright, a rope tied about his neck, and an intimation of his fate given him by the spokesman of the party. Garrett called aloud to the Jailer, who was detained above, "Oh, Toothman! Oh, Toothman!" The Jailer answered, "Garrett, I can't help you now," for he was heavily guarded, but making an effort to get below, was struck a savage blow in the forehead and felled to the floor.

A PRISONER'S STORY.

A prisoner who is confined on the lower floor, and within four feet of this scene, says Garrett fought like a tiger, exclaiming repeatedly, "I know you,——! I know you,——!" The prisoner, however, as well as the Jailer, fails to be able to give the names that should fill the above blanks. No wonder; all were frightened, and all this terrible tragedy was enacted in a few minutes. After this the only sound heard was a gurgling noise made by the doomed man as he was dragged from the Jail by the rope around his neck.

He was hung to a maple in the front of he Jail, over a limb some sixteen feet from he ground. The rope used was a common cotton clothes-line. The mob came fully prepared, and the person who affixed the rope to the limb was shod with what telegraph men term "climbers."

PRECAUTIONS.

The guard who had the Jailer in charge upon leaving, warned him that if he showed his head within twenty minutes it should be "blown off." The poor turnkey, in trembling fright, was willing to obey, but his wife having native curiosity regarding the movement outside, crept to the garret and after three or four minutes (by her time) announced that the party had gone, and that the coast was clear. Then he essayed forth and summoned the Sheriff and Coroner who, together with the Sentinel representative, were soon upon the ground.

Lynchings are occurring with alarming frequency. A few months ago Illinois, Wisconsin and Michigan joined the border states and the territories in substituting mob violence for the action of the courts. A few weeks ago there was a lynching in Indiana which was attended by such adjuncts of a legal execution as a clergyman and a surgeon. Wednesday night two men were lynched together in Kentucky, two together in one town in Colorado, and one in another, and at an early hour yesterday morning a man was lynched in Minneapolis. In all these cases but one there is little or no doubt about the guilt of the victims, but in one case a man was lynched on suspicion, and in Indiana only a week ago a man was hanged by a mob after he had been tried by a jury and acquitted. These violent and lawless proceedings raise once more the question, Is civilization a failure?

It is no justification of a murder by a mob that the victim deserves hanging. The only case of these recent cases in which there is any approach to justification is that occurred in Minneapolis. There the mob killed a man who had committed as atrocious a crime as can be conceived of, but one for which it was not at all likely that he could be legally hanged. In all the other cases the penalty of the law was sufficient. The worst case of all was the one in Indiana, where a mob murdered a man who had been tried and found innocent by a jury. To justify or in any degree excuse that act would be equivalent to the obliteration of all criminal courts and procedure, and the return to the methods of savages. The man may have been guilty, in spite of the verdict, but if verdicts are to be disregarded, and if people are to hang every man whom they think a scoundrel merely because they think so, and without regard to legal evidence, then there is an end to organized society, and to the security of life and property, and social chaos and barbarism are already introduced. Civilization involves something more than the punishment of criminals; criminals are punished by Indians and Hottentots. It involves the ascertainment of guilt by rules of evidence, the execution of the penalties of the law by authorized persons, and the settlement of disputes between man and man, and between society and the individual, by duly-organized courts.

The fact that a hundred men can vent their rage against an evil-doer with impunity incites a hundred men in another locality to do the same thing. These frequent lynchings in comparatively old and established communities, where all the instrumentalities for the legal punishment of crime exist, are not sporadic outbreaks of inflamed public sentiment. They are the symptoms of an epidemic. They beget contempt for the courts and a spirit of defiance to the law. Tuesday morning the people of Las Vegas were again shocked by the news of the cowardly murder of Frank Mayer, an inoffensive old German, who has followed the butcher business in this city for several years. He was a man of kind disposition and as honest as the day is long, his only failing being that he liked beer a little too well and, therefore, indulged in its use a little too frequent for his own good, though it never rendered him boisterous, but on the contrary made him more good-humored and jovial than ever. During last winter he employed H. C. Brown to butcher at his slaughter house. One day Mr. Mayer missed a dressed beef. Taking the trail of the wagon, he found where the beef had been sold. He at once had Brown arrested and tried for the offense. Brown was found guilty and sentenced to three months imprisonment in the county jail. This term expired a few days ago, and when Brown was let out of jail he breathed numerous threats against Mayer.

Immediately before coming to this city he got into trouble with another butcher, and served him in a similar manner to the way he served Mayer, striking his victim that time with a six-shooter. For this offence he had to leave Trinidad.

Chicago is again afflicted with one of those crime epidemics that periodically break out in that city, and killings are almost of daily occurrence. Encounter Between Whites and Blacks in Florida-Three Negroes Killed.
JACKSONVILLA Fla. July 1-The Union
Encounter Between Whites and Blacks in Florida—Three Negroes Killed.
JACKSONVILLE, Fla., July 1.—The Union has just received the particulars of a fatal encounter between the whites and blacks at Brookville. Three colored men named Turner had been for several days visiting the village armed, and indulging in threats against some of the citizens, making much bad feeling. This culminated a few days since in a row in the court house, started by one of the Turners entering the building just as the afternoon session of the court was being called, with an open knife in his hand. In the row that followed the three Turners were killed and several other negroes participating were wounded. Several whites were wounded, but not mortally.

The following particulars of the fatal row at Brooksville, Florida, brief mention of which was made in the MORNING NEWS of the 1st instant, we find in the Jacksonville Union of Sunday last:

"Last Sunday night a young man by the name of Stringfellow walked into Hancock's barroom, where quite a number of negroes had collected, and in making his way to the counter, pushed a negro named Tom Johnson out of his way. As he turned to go out the negro followed and asked if Stringfellow intended to insult him. Being assured that no insult was intended, he walked off, but as Stringfellow stepped from the door Jim Turner, a mulatto negro, grabbed him by the throat, and asked what he meant by shoving people around, at the same time knocking him down and cutting his head with a pistol. A general row was imminent, when the Marshal interfered, and made several arrests. In the melee Jim Turner escaped, but was arrested Sunday afternoon. Monday morning the Turners were here in force, all armed, and making a great many threats. Owing to a want of evidence, the case was dismissed. During the afternoon Rube Turner drew his pistol on Mr. Quinn; Marshal Hancock disarmed and arrested both parties. Tuesday Henry and Rube Turner renewed the difficulty with Mr. Quinn, Henry presenting a double barreleen gun at that gentleman. Again the Marshal interfered, arresting both parties. Wednesday Jim, Henry and Rube Turner all came in town armed, and it became evident that mischief was brewing, and the white people began to make preparations to meet it. By two o'clock in the afternoon there were at least fifty negroes in town. All went on quietly until about five o'clock, when there was a little ripple of excitement.

"On the adjournment of the court of investigation, about sundown, the crowd dispersed, and everything was quiet until this morning. On the calling of court this morning, the Turner gang, with their followers, were here in force, and all well armed. The whites were apparently unsuspectious, but one accustomed to watch men could see that they were prepared for any emergency. In view of the large number of armed and turbulent negroes in town (between fifty and seventy-five), the Mayor appointed five or six special police to aid the Marshal and his deputy in keeping down any disturbance. Everything moved along quietly until court was called for the afternoon session.

"While the Marshal was calling court Jim and Henry Turner entered the court house, Henry with an open knife in his hand. What he said or did I am unable to find out, but a row was the immediate result. Nor can I learn who fired the first shot. It was, however, fired in the court house. When the firing commenced and the negroes discovered a perfect understanding and discipline among the whites, they scattered in all directions, making but a slight attempt to sustain their leaders. A few of them opened fire as the row commenced, but the well directed shots of the whites soon convinced them that safety lay in flight, and a rapid one at that. To sum up, the three Turners (negroes) were killed outright; several other negroes were wounded; two white men were very slightly wounded, and one powder-burned in the eye. This difficulty has been pending for the past two years, and nothing but the utmost forbearance on the part of the whites has kept it off this long."

From the McMinnville New Era.]
Last Wednesday evening, while a negro woman, living near where Capt. James M. Davis was recently assassinated, was in the woods near where the murder took place gathering ginseng, she found a large-sized navy pistol, with all the chambers loaded. The woman brought the pistol home and delivered it to Mr. Phelps, on whose place she was living. Last Friday night, two days after the pistol was found, eight masked men went to her cabin and demanded the pistol; she told them that she did not have it. They then demanded, with threats, to know where the pistol was; she told them Mr. Phelps had it. They repaired to the house of Phelps, and calling him up to the window, demanded the pistol found by the negro woman, which de delivered to them through the window. It is very natural to suppose that the party demanding the pistol were engaged in or were in possession of facts concerning the killing of Davis, and were apprehensive the pistol might be an agent in ferring them out, and hence their determination to regain it. It might have been fortunate for the ends of justice had Mr. Phelps at once delivered the pistol into the hands of the authorities; but having it in his possession it is more than likely any of us would have acceded to the demands made upon him for its possession. But even the finding of the pistol, and its subsequent recovery by its owner, may yet furnish a clue to the perpetrators of the murder. We believe it will yet out.

A Young Double Murderer.

John Tribbett, a boy fifteen years of age, was arrested at the levee Thursday morning by Sheriff Butler, of Ottertail county, Minn., and lodged in our county jail. He is charged with the murder of two men at Perham, in the county mentioned. The circumstances of the murder are given below. They were gleaned from a telegram received at the Tribune office yesterday. It appears that on Monday, the 30th ult., that a surveyor who came up there from Michigan, started out about that time to survey some land located several miles from that town, and took with him a German boy named Fritz, belonging to that vicinity. While out they were joined by a lad named John Tribbett, aged fifteen, a boy of quarrelsome and bad character, who had been working in the woods during the winter. Tribbett was well known, but regarded as a worthless vagabond. On Monday Tribbett borrowed a gun from a neighbor, who shortly afterwards heard some shots, but thought nothing of it. Later Tribbett came into town with the surveyor's watch and a revolver. He sold the watch for five dollars to the city marshal. It is supposed that on the same night or Tuesday morning he left for the west, which supposition has proven well founded. On Friday the dead body of the German boy Fritz was discovered by a farmer, the head crushed in, several bullet holes in the body, and a fatal knife wound in the neck. This led to a search for the surveyor, whose body was found that evening. The young villian arrived here last Saturday evening and went under the alias of Ford. When he left the scene of the murder he had about $90, but upon arriving here he was broke, as on yesterday he pawned a revolver to John Ludwig and then proceeded to the levee, and while engaged in a conversation with the captain of the ferry boat Undine the officer rode on the steamer and captured his game. A reporter for the TRIBUNE called at the jail last evening and had an interview with the prisoner. He appeared cheerful and gave the turnkey a cigar. The writer informed him that he desired his statement of the affair with which he was charged, and upon a moments reflection replied that according to his experience statements were only made to lawyers by big men, and he thought he would imitate his seniors. But after being assured that it would not prejudice his case by claiming his innocence, he still insisted upon refusing, which in itself was a confession of guilt.

Young Tribbett, who is only fifteen years and one month old, is as villainous a specimen of a dime novel reader as one could discover in a year's hunt. He is large, coarse and brutal in appearance.

During a conversation with Geo. Thomas, the jailor, the TRIBUNE was informed by that gentleman that the murderer had confessed to him to the extent that he was not alone in the murder, that the blame was not all on him. He is evidently the one wanted.

The information that has come into the possession of the TRIBUNE regarding the boy, John Tibbitts, who was arrested in this city Monday, charged with the murder of two men at Perham, Minn., proves him to be the most brutal human fiend that ever walked the earth. At the jail Monday night he told the prisoners that had his gun not been in soak, the officer who arrested him would have gone back to Perham in a box. And while in the car Wednesday morning, by which he went east, he remarked to the conductor: "For Jesus Christ's sake, conductor, shut that door and charge an admission fee, and when we reach Fargo we'll have a bully good time." He admitted that he didn't expect to live long after reaching the scene of the murder.

A telegram to the Pioneer Press, from Perham, states that he hacked the Dutch boy, one of the two victims, in a horrible manner with an ax, giving him over twenty wounds after shooting him and cutting his throat with a knife. One or more of the ax wounds went clear through his ribs to the handle.

According to the laws of Minnesota, this young fiend can only receive a punishment of five years' imprisonment in the reform school, until he is twenty years of age. If the laws of that state are as they have been expounded here, a youth nineteen years and ten months old could commit murder in that state and be at liberty before his trial begun. If he can't be hung, he should surely be lynched, and that will probably be his fate.

An interview with a gentleman from Perham says: "New facts in the Perham murder case are continually coming to light. She exhibited no signs of grief when told that her son was lynched, nor did she view the body or seem to care to see it. Young Tibbets's stepfather has shown greater feeling than the boy's mother, and the public generally sympathize with him. Public feeling is strongly in sympathy with the lynching. EDITOR JOURNAL: I have twenty minutes in which to write you the eventful happenings of this city in the last 24 hours. When I arrived here this morning at 10 o'clock about the first thing I saw after the man who shouted, "Right this way for the Grand Central Hotel," was a man hanging from a telegraph pole with a rope around his neck. Upon inquiry I found he was Wm. Graham, who murdered his uncle and set fire to his shanty, in the northwest part of this county, about 5 days ago. All for $125. He was confined in the jail here, and had confessed his crime.

Monday evening, at 9 o'clock, a party of masked horsemen rode rapidly and quietly into town, hitched their horses at a convenient point and made a determined break for the jail. The active parties engaged were perhaps 25. It was generally understood during the afternoon that something of the kind would occur during the night. There were 300 witnesses to the tragedy.

A Young Man Abducted from a Saloon and Not Seen Since.
ATCHISON, KAN., March 13.—The facts about the mysterious disappearance of Walter Saunders, a popular young citizen of Atchison, have been given by John Kennedy, an eye-witness of the abduction. Saunders was addicted to drink, and lost his position for indulgence in this habit. He went to Kansas city to clerk in a prominent boot and shoe-store there. Last Monday he, Edward Toller, book-keeper for Fowler Brothers, of Kansas city, and others, were drinking in a saloon, when four men rushed into the place, grabbed Saunders and forcibly dragged him from his friends. He was hurried up a dark alley by the party, now increased to twelve. His friends pursued and found that the mob had taken Saunders to a house, and there, in the presence of a thirteen-year-old girl named Flanagan, accused him of assaulting her. Saunders made no reply to the charge. He was then taken to the street and hurried in the direction of the Kaw bridge, and as he has never been heard from since it is supposed that he was thrown into the river. This supposition is strengthened by the fact that Ellet, one of two brothers strung up in order to force him to tell what had become of the missing man, said that he turned his back when they made away with him.
